newsitem.title: USA: IMF leaves open question of gold sales -- again.
newsitem.headline: IMF leaves open question of gold sales -- again.

text.p: The IMF's policy-making Interim Committee pledged on Sunday to find the money needed to finance stepped-up aid to the world's poorest nations, but stopped short of spelling out where the funds would come from.

The decision, announced in a communique issued after a day of talks, effectively left open the question of whether the International Monetary Fund will eventually sell off some of its gold for that purpose.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus, backed up by the United States and most of the Fund's member nations, has proposed selling up to five million ounces of gold.
But a handful of other nations, particularly Germany, are opposed, and instead want the IMF to use contributions from its member nations to finance the increased aid.

Camdessus said on Sunday he had the 85-percent majority of board members needed to approve a gold sale. But he made clear he did not want to isolate Germany with a divisive vote and voiced hopes that a decision could eventually be reached by consensus.
Germany, though, did not sound very conciliatory.
"Our position holds," German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told reporters on Sunday.

"It is unrealistic and counterproductive for the IMF ... to rely on bilateral contributions ... as the Fund is sitting on nearly $40 billion worth of gold that is illiquid," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told the Interim Committee.
The issue is not particularly pressing, as the IMF has
enough money in its kitty to last until 1999 or 2000.

On Saturday, a senior Canadian Finance Ministry official suggested that gold sales might not be needed until 1998 or after. But on Sunday, his boss, Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin, urged the IMF to proceed with gold sales soon.
"I would like to see the IMF Executive Board endorse the sale of five million ounces of gold sooner rather than later," Martin told the Interim Committee.
Any sale, he added, should be carried out "in a gradual and transparent manner. This will ensure that the impact on world gold markets is negligible."
The IMF has sold gold before, in the 1970's, through public auctions, to help poor countries cope with the oil price shock.
